paragraphs.title: Achan's sin and the Lord's anger

easy.question: Who violated the 'accursed thing' according to the verse?
answers: The children of Israel
Joshua
the Canaanites
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing' — it identifies Israel as the ones who broke the ban.

easy.question: Who took of the accursed thing according to the verse?
answers: the whole tribe of Judah
Achan son of Carmi
the entire people
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly names 'Achan son of Carmi' as the one who took the accursed thing.

easy.question: What was the LORD's reaction to Israel in this verse?
answers: The LORD blessed them
The LORD ignored them
The LORD's anger was kindled
easy.explanation: The verse says 'and the anger of the Lord was kindled' — the LORD was angry with the people.

medium.question: Why is this theft described as a serious offense that provokes the LORD's anger?
answers: Because they broke a divine ban — a command that forbids taking certain items
Because they did not observe the Sabbath
Because they lost a military battle
medium.explanation: The verse emphasizes 'committed a trespass in the accursed thing' — they violated a divine ban (herem), and breaking a divine command provokes God's anger.

medium.question: What does the term 'the accursed thing' mean in this context (verse uses the phrase 'the accursed thing')?
answers: An area of land forbidden for use
An object or property devoted for destruction or reserved for God — forbidden for ordinary use
A local family name
medium.explanation: In context 'the accursed thing' refers to property set aside by divine command (often to be destroyed or dedicated to God), and Achan taking it shows he took what was forbidden.

medium.question: From which tribe was Achan according to the verse?
answers: the tribe of Levi
the tribe of Reuben
the tribe of Judah
medium.explanation: The verse specifies 'of the tribe of Judah' — Achan belonged to Judah.

challenge.question: What does the expression 'the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing' signify socially and morally?
answers: That this was a private offense with no effect on others
That the sin was considered a collective harm and had consequences for the whole people
That the ban was transferred to the enemies
challenge.explanation: The wording treats the act as a communal offense (by 'the children of Israel'), and the wider narrative shows that one person's sin exposed the whole nation to punishment — a collective responsibility.

challenge.question: Why does the verse list Achan's genealogy ('son of Carmi son of Zabdi son of Zerah')?
answers: To praise his family
To conceal his real identity
To identify the person precisely and place him within his family and tribe
challenge.explanation: The genealogy serves to identify the individual precisely and show his family and tribal affiliation — important for investigation and public responsibility in that period.

challenge.question: In the cultural-religious context of conquest stories, what is the role of a 'herem' (ban) as seen here?
answers: A sacred command to set aside or devote items or people to the LORD, sometimes by destruction
A kind of tax the people must pay
An agricultural custom for distributing the harvest
challenge.explanation: In biblical tradition a 'herem' is a divine command to devote items or peoples — often to destruction — as a holy act; violating it is a grave religious offense.

questions.question: What does the expression 'the children of Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing' signify socially and morally?
answers: That this was a private offense with no effect on others
That the sin was considered a collective harm and had consequences for the whole people
That the ban was transferred to the enemies
questions.explanation: The wording treats the act as a communal offense (by 'the children of Israel'), and the wider narrative shows that one person's sin exposed the whole nation to punishment — a collective responsibility.

questions.question: Why does the verse list Achan's genealogy ('son of Carmi son of Zabdi son of Zerah')?
answers: To praise his family
To conceal his real identity
To identify the person precisely and place him within his family and tribe
questions.explanation: The genealogy serves to identify the individual precisely and show his family and tribal affiliation — important for investigation and public responsibility in that period.

questions.question: In the cultural-religious context of conquest stories, what is the role of a 'herem' (ban) as seen here?
answers: A sacred command to set aside or devote items or people to the LORD, sometimes by destruction
A kind of tax the people must pay
An agricultural custom for distributing the harvest
questions.explanation: In biblical tradition a 'herem' is a divine command to devote items or peoples — often to destruction — as a holy act; violating it is a grave religious offense.

easy.question: To which city did Joshua send men to scout the land?
answers: Jericho
Ai
Bethel
easy.explanation: The text says Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai to spy out the city — Ai was the scouting target.

easy.question: What did the scouts advise about how many men should go up to take Ai?
answers: About two or three thousand would suffice
All the people should go up
They should not attack at all
easy.explanation: They said 'not all the people should go up... about two or three thousand' — recommending 2–3 thousand men.

easy.question: How many men actually went up to fight Ai?
answers: One thousand
Six thousand
About three thousand
easy.explanation: The verse reports 'about three thousand men' went up.

medium.question: What was the scouts' recommendation regarding sending forces against Ai?
answers: Send only a few thousand, not the whole nation
Send the entire nation to ensure victory
Avoid battle and negotiate
medium.explanation: The spies recommended 'not all the people... about two or three thousand' — a limited force of 2–3 thousand.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'their hearts melted' mean in this context (the verse uses 'became as water')?
answers: Their hearts grew weak/they were terrified and demoralized
Their hearts were filled with joy
Their hearts were strengthened and became firm
medium.explanation: The image 'became as water' is metaphorical: it means the people's courage melted away — they were frightened and demoralized after the rout.

medium.question: Why did our soldiers flee before the men of Ai?
answers: They were defeated in battle and some were killed, causing a rout and panic
They had decided to withdraw the night before the battle
They were ordered to return and not fight
medium.explanation: They were routed and pursued; the text describes them fleeing and being chased, producing panic and a collapse in morale.

challenge.question: The verse describes Ai as 'on the east of Bethel.' What does that geographical phrase indicate?
answers: That Ai was west of Bethel
That Ai lay to the east of Bethel
That Ai was north of Bethel
challenge.explanation: The phrase places Ai relative to Bethel: 'on the east of Bethel' indicates it was east of/beyond Bethel.

challenge.question: What is the figurative suggestion of the phrase 'became as water' at the end of the verse?
answers: They became numerous like water
The people's resolve dissolved — their hearts melted and they faded in fear
They flowed down like water in a valley
challenge.explanation: The expression conveys moral/spiritual collapse: their courage dissolved and they melted away in fear — a common biblical metaphor for collapse.

challenge.question: Why does the verse emphasize the relatively small number killed (36) although the rout affected about 3,000 who went up?
answers: To show that psychological defeat and the ensuing rout had broad consequences beyond the raw casualty count
Because the number 36 carried secret ritual significance
To stress that each death was singled out and emphasized
challenge.explanation: Although only 36 were killed, the psychological impact of the defeat and pursuit caused a wider collapse of morale and a large-scale rout, so the small death toll did not lessen the overall disaster.

questions.question: The verse describes Ai as 'on the east of Bethel.' What does that geographical phrase indicate?
answers: That Ai was west of Bethel
That Ai lay to the east of Bethel
That Ai was north of Bethel
questions.explanation: The phrase places Ai relative to Bethel: 'on the east of Bethel' indicates it was east of/beyond Bethel.

questions.question: What is the figurative suggestion of the phrase 'became as water' at the end of the verse?
answers: They became numerous like water
The people's resolve dissolved — their hearts melted and they faded in fear
They flowed down like water in a valley
questions.explanation: The expression conveys moral/spiritual collapse: their courage dissolved and they melted away in fear — a common biblical metaphor for collapse.

questions.question: Why does the verse emphasize the relatively small number killed (36) although the rout affected about 3,000 who went up?
answers: To show that psychological defeat and the ensuing rout had broad consequences beyond the raw casualty count
Because the number 36 carried secret ritual significance
To stress that each death was singled out and emphasized
questions.explanation: Although only 36 were killed, the psychological impact of the defeat and pursuit caused a wider collapse of morale and a large-scale rout, so the small death toll did not lessen the overall disaster.

easy.question: Who tore his clothes and fell on his face according to the verses?
answers: Moses
Joshua
Aaron
easy.explanation: Verse 6 explicitly says Joshua rent his clothes and fell on his face before the ark of the LORD.

easy.question: Where did Joshua fall on his face?
answers: Before the ark of the LORD
outside the camp
on the banks of the Jordan
easy.explanation: The verse states he fell 'before the ark of the LORD' — that is the location.

easy.question: What did the elders of Israel do in verse 6?
answers: Offer a sacrifice
Sing liturgical songs
Put dust on their heads
easy.explanation: The verse reports 'they put dust upon their heads' — a sign of mourning and repentance.

medium.question: Why does Joshua say, 'Wherefore hast thou brought this people over Jordan, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us?'
answers: Because he fears the crossing has led them to destruction by the Amorites
Because he is glad about the crossing and wants to bless them
Because he desires to return to exile
medium.explanation: Joshua expresses anguish that crossing the Jordan might have led them into disaster at the hands of the Amorites, as he says in verse 7.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'turned their backs' mean in the context 'when Israel turneth their backs before their enemies' (v.8)?
answers: To turn the neck — to flee or retreat from the enemy
To face the enemy and attack
An internal change of heart
medium.explanation: Here 'turn their backs' describes retreating or fleeing from the enemy rather than standing to fight.

medium.question: What central concern does Joshua express regarding the LORD's reputation in verse 9?
answers: That people will build a new temple for the LORD
That the LORD's name will be dishonored if the people are cut off from the land
That the LORD will lose kingship
medium.explanation: Joshua fears that if Israel is destroyed and their name wiped out, the LORD's great name will be blemished among the nations — he worries about God's reputation.

challenge.question: What does Joshua's tearing of garments and falling on his face until evening suggest about his leadership style?
answers: That he was indifferent to the crisis
That he took responsibility, mourned, and entreated the LORD
That he was planning a tactical retreat
challenge.explanation: Those actions are signs of mourning and prayer — Joshua accepts responsibility, laments the situation, and petitions God rather than merely issuing military orders.

challenge.question: What is the cultural meaning of 'putting dust on their heads' by the elders of Israel?
answers: A sign of royal coronation
A sign of celebration and thanksgiving
A sign of grief, repentance, and seeking forgiveness
challenge.explanation: In biblical practice, throwing dust on one's head is a sign of mourning and penitence; here the elders express sorrow and awe over the situation.

challenge.question: What does the passage warn will happen if Israel turns their backs and the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear of it?
answers: They will make peace with Israel and live securely
They will surround Israel, attack them, and cut off their name from the land
They will come to Israel's aid against the Amorites
challenge.explanation: The text warns that the Canaanites and inhabitants will hear and surround Israel, leading to their destruction or erasure from the land — 'cut off our name from the earth'.

questions.question: What does Joshua's tearing of garments and falling on his face until evening suggest about his leadership style?
answers: That he was indifferent to the crisis
That he took responsibility, mourned, and entreated the LORD
That he was planning a tactical retreat
questions.explanation: Those actions are signs of mourning and prayer — Joshua accepts responsibility, laments the situation, and petitions God rather than merely issuing military orders.

questions.question: What is the cultural meaning of 'putting dust on their heads' by the elders of Israel?
answers: A sign of royal coronation
A sign of celebration and thanksgiving
A sign of grief, repentance, and seeking forgiveness
questions.explanation: In biblical practice, throwing dust on one's head is a sign of mourning and penitence; here the elders express sorrow and awe over the situation.

questions.question: What does the passage warn will happen if Israel turns their backs and the Canaanites and all who live in the land hear of it?
answers: They will make peace with Israel and live securely
They will surround Israel, attack them, and cut off their name from the land
They will come to Israel's aid against the Amorites
questions.explanation: The text warns that the Canaanites and inhabitants will hear and surround Israel, leading to their destruction or erasure from the land — 'cut off our name from the earth'.

paragraphs.title: Revelation of the guilt and instructions for purification

easy.question: Who spoke to Joshua in verse 10?
answers: Moses
the LORD
Aaron
easy.explanation: Verse 10 explicitly says 'And the LORD said unto Joshua' — the speaker is the LORD.

easy.question: What had Israel done according to verses 11–12?
answers: They sinned, broke the covenant, and took of the accursed thing
They won a decisive victory over their enemies
They erected foreign altars
easy.explanation: The passage states 'Israel hath sinned... and they have taken of the accursed thing' — they violated the covenant and took the herem.

easy.question: What will happen to the person who is found 'taken with the accursed thing' according to verse 15?
answers: He will be exiled
He will be tried only by a court
He shall be burnt with fire
easy.explanation: Verse 15 declares 'he that is taken with the accursed thing shall be burnt with fire' — the punishment is burning.

medium.question: Why, according to these verses, could the Israelites not stand before their enemies?
answers: Because they lacked sufficient weapons
Because Joshua feared to fight
Because the accursed thing was among them and the LORD would not be with them until it was destroyed
medium.explanation: The text says Israelites could not stand because of the accursed thing among them; God's presence and help were withheld until the accursed thing was removed.

medium.question: What is the order of the inspection the people should undergo to find the guilty party (verse 14)?
answers: They will be brought according to tribes; the tribe according to families; the family according to households; the household man by man
They will be called by personal names
Leaders will inspect each family randomly
medium.explanation: Verse 14 describes a stepwise process: tribes, then families, then households, then individuals — a hierarchical selection for identification.

medium.question: What does the term 'the accursed thing' mean here (the verse says 'There is an accursed thing in the midst of thee')?
answers: A gift reserved exclusively for the priests
An item devoted to destruction or dedicated to God (forbidden to use)
Ordinary booty from war
medium.explanation: The context — commands to destroy the accursed thing and the penalty — shows it is property devoted to God or destruction, not a regular item to be used.

challenge.question: What theological meaning is conveyed by 'I will no more be with you' unless you destroy the accursed thing?
answers: That military success depends on ritual purity and covenant faithfulness: God's presence is conditional on obedience to the covenant
That God will remain with them regardless of their actions
That it is merely a tactical threat to intimidate the people
challenge.explanation: The statement indicates God's presence and support are conditional on the people's obedience; the removal of the offense is necessary for God's continued aid.

challenge.question: What does the punishment 'shall be burnt with fire, he and all that he hath' imply about the gravity of the offense?
answers: That the punishment is mild and local
That it is the same as ordinary civil penalties
That it is severe and includes forfeiture of possessions — the offense is a serious breach of the covenant
challenge.explanation: Burning the person and all his possessions signals a severe sanction and complete removal of the offense from the community, indicating the gravity of violating the covenant.

challenge.question: What does the use of a lottery-like selection order (tribe → family → household → man) indicate about Israelite social structure at that time?
answers: That tribe and family were important units of responsibility and social connection
That society functioned entirely as unrelated individuals
That this is a modern democratic election method
challenge.explanation: The stepwise process highlights the centrality of tribe and family as social and legal units — responsibility and identity were organized around these groups.

questions.question: What theological meaning is conveyed by 'I will no more be with you' unless you destroy the accursed thing?
answers: That military success depends on ritual purity and covenant faithfulness: God's presence is conditional on obedience to the covenant
That God will remain with them regardless of their actions
That it is merely a tactical threat to intimidate the people
questions.explanation: The statement indicates God's presence and support are conditional on the people's obedience; the removal of the offense is necessary for God's continued aid.

questions.question: What does the punishment 'shall be burnt with fire, he and all that he hath' imply about the gravity of the offense?
answers: That the punishment is mild and local
That it is the same as ordinary civil penalties
That it is severe and includes forfeiture of possessions — the offense is a serious breach of the covenant
questions.explanation: Burning the person and all his possessions signals a severe sanction and complete removal of the offense from the community, indicating the gravity of violating the covenant.

questions.question: What does the use of a lottery-like selection order (tribe → family → household → man) indicate about Israelite social structure at that time?
answers: That tribe and family were important units of responsibility and social connection
That society functioned entirely as unrelated individuals
That this is a modern democratic election method
questions.explanation: The stepwise process highlights the centrality of tribe and family as social and legal units — responsibility and identity were organized around these groups.

easy.question: Which tribe was selected when Joshua brought Israel by their tribes (v.16)?
answers: the tribe of Judah
the tribe of Ephraim
the tribe of Benjamin
easy.explanation: Verse 16 states the tribe of Judah was taken — Judah was selected.

easy.question: Which family within that tribe was picked (v.17)?
answers: Achan
Zabdi
Carmi
easy.explanation: Verse 17 names Zabdi as the one taken from the family of the Zarhites.

easy.question: What did Joshua ask Achan to do in verse 19?
answers: To praise himself
To flee from the place
Give glory to the LORD, make confession, and tell me what you have done
easy.explanation: Joshua said 'give, I pray thee, glory to the LORD... and tell me now what thou hast done' — he asked for confession and honor to God.

medium.question: What sequence of inspection does Joshua follow until he reaches the guilty man (vv.16–18)?
answers: Tribes → families → family of the Zarhites → households → individual
Houses → tribes → families → individual
Tribes → families → yards/households → individual
medium.explanation: The passage shows a hierarchical process: tribes, then families, then households/men — tribes → families → households → individuals.

medium.question: In the phrase 'give glory to the LORD' (v.19), what does 'glory' mean in this context?
answers: Honor, praise, and recognition
A heavy weight
A tax/payment
medium.explanation: Joshua asks Achan to give honor and praise to the LORD and to confess — 'glory' indicates honor/tribute to God.

medium.question: What does the listing 'Achan son of Carmi son of Zabdi son of Zerah' indicate (vv.18–19)?
answers: Cities where Achan lived
A list of enemies who fought Judah
Achan's family/lineage within the tribe of Judah
medium.explanation: The names show his genealogy — identifying his family line and tribal affiliation within Judah.

challenge.question: Why likely did Joshua rise early and assemble the people by their tribes (inferred from v.16 and context)?
answers: To perform a morning sacrifice
To discover who had sinned and mete out responsibility
To organize another military sortie the same day
challenge.explanation: Gathering by tribes and the subsequent questioning indicate the aim was to identify the offender responsible for the failure.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'and make confession unto him' (v.19) likely represent in a ritual-historical sense?
answers: A thank-offering or formal confession before the LORD
A financial tax payment to the tribal treasury
An order to pay a fine to an enemy altar
challenge.explanation: In biblical usage 'confession' can mean a formal acknowledgment before God — here a public admission or offering before the LORD.

challenge.question: To which tribe did Achan belong according to these verses?
answers: All Israel generally, without tribal identification
the tribe of Judah
the tribe of Ephraim
challenge.explanation: Verses 18–19 identify Achan 'of the tribe of Judah' — he belonged to Judah.

questions.question: Why likely did Joshua rise early and assemble the people by their tribes (inferred from v.16 and context)?
answers: To perform a morning sacrifice
To discover who had sinned and mete out responsibility
To organize another military sortie the same day
questions.explanation: Gathering by tribes and the subsequent questioning indicate the aim was to identify the offender responsible for the failure.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'and make confession unto him' (v.19) likely represent in a ritual-historical sense?
answers: A thank-offering or formal confession before the LORD
A financial tax payment to the tribal treasury
An order to pay a fine to an enemy altar
questions.explanation: In biblical usage 'confession' can mean a formal acknowledgment before God — here a public admission or offering before the LORD.

questions.question: To which tribe did Achan belong according to these verses?
answers: All Israel generally, without tribal identification
the tribe of Judah
the tribe of Ephraim
questions.explanation: Verses 18–19 identify Achan 'of the tribe of Judah' — he belonged to Judah.

paragraphs.title: Confession and the discovery of the spoil

easy.question: Who confessed the offense in verse 20?
answers: Achan
Joshua
all Israel
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'And Achan answered Joshua...' — Achan confessed.

easy.question: Which items did Achan report that he had taken in verse 21?
answers: Only a garment
A Babylonish garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold
Only small change
easy.explanation: He names 'a goodly Babylonish garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold' — those are the items.

easy.question: Where were the items found according to the verses?
answers: In a pit outside the camp
In the king's courtyard
Hidden in his tent and the silver under it
easy.explanation: He said they were 'hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it' — hidden in his tent with the silver beneath.

medium.question: Why did Joshua send messengers to the tent?
answers: To bless the family
To recover what Achan confessed to having taken
To guard the camp at night
medium.explanation: After Achan's confession, Joshua sent messengers to check the tent and recover the confessed items.

medium.question: In the phrase 'I coveted them, and took them' (v.21), what does 'coveted' mean in this context?
answers: I hid them
I destroyed them
I desired them and longed to take them
medium.explanation: 'Coveted' means he strongly desired the items and therefore stole them; it expresses wrongful desire leading to action.

medium.question: What did the Israelites do with the recovered items after they found them?
answers: They returned them to Achan and kept silent
They laid them out before Joshua and before the LORD
They re-hidden them in the camp
medium.explanation: They took the items out, brought them to Joshua and all Israel, and laid them out before the LORD.

challenge.question: Why was Achan brought with his possessions to the Valley of Achor according to the context?
answers: For honor and celebration
To return him home
To remove him from the camp and present him for judgment and punishment
challenge.explanation: He and all his goods were taken out to the valley as part of public judgment and to remove the offense from the community.

challenge.question: What does the mention of a 'Babylonish garment' among the spoils suggest about the nature of the booty?
answers: That the spoil included items from distant regions like Shinar/Babylon
That 'Babylonish' is simply a local family name
That the garment was actually currency rather than clothing
challenge.explanation: 'Babylonish' (or Shinar) indicates foreign origin; the spoil included luxury items from distant lands, not only local goods.

challenge.question: What did Joshua take from Achan at the end of the account in these verses?
answers: Only the silver and the garment
Achan himself, the silver, the garment, the wedge of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen and other possessions, and his tent
Only his children
challenge.explanation: The text lists that Joshua took Achan, his silver, garment, wedge of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen, donkeys, sheep, tent, and all he had.

questions.question: Why was Achan brought with his possessions to the Valley of Achor according to the context?
answers: For honor and celebration
To return him home
To remove him from the camp and present him for judgment and punishment
questions.explanation: He and all his goods were taken out to the valley as part of public judgment and to remove the offense from the community.

questions.question: What does the mention of a 'Babylonish garment' among the spoils suggest about the nature of the booty?
answers: That the spoil included items from distant regions like Shinar/Babylon
That 'Babylonish' is simply a local family name
That the garment was actually currency rather than clothing
questions.explanation: 'Babylonish' (or Shinar) indicates foreign origin; the spoil included luxury items from distant lands, not only local goods.

questions.question: What did Joshua take from Achan at the end of the account in these verses?
answers: Only the silver and the garment
Achan himself, the silver, the garment, the wedge of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen and other possessions, and his tent
Only his children
questions.explanation: The text lists that Joshua took Achan, his silver, garment, wedge of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen, donkeys, sheep, tent, and all he had.

easy.question: What did all Israel do to the man who was found guilty (v.25)?
answers: They stoned him and burned him with fire
They embraced him and forgave him
They only exiled him
easy.explanation: The verse describes that they stoned him and burned them with fire after stoning — the people executed the punishment.

easy.question: What did they raise over him after executing the sentence (v.26)?
answers: A personal monument in his honor
A great heap of stones
An altar on which to sacrifice
easy.explanation: They 'raised over him a great heap of stones' — a large pile (a mound) of stones was erected.

easy.question: What happened to the LORD's fierce anger after they carried out the punishment and set up the heap of stones?
answers: The LORD became more furious
The people were immediately exiled
The LORD turned from his fierceness of anger
easy.explanation: Verse 26 says 'So the LORD turned from the fierceness of his anger' — God's anger ceased after the act.

medium.question: What is the sequence of events in verses 25–26?
answers: They stoned, burned, and then raised the heap of stones over him
They raised the heap of stones first, then stoned and burned
They burned him first, then raised the heap, but did not stone him
medium.explanation: The passage describes the execution (stoning and burning) and then says they raised a great heap of stones over him.

medium.question: What does the question 'Why hast thou troubled us?' (Joshua's address to Achan) mean in this context (paraphrase)?
answers: Moving something from one place to another
You have caused us harm/profanation and brought disaster on the community
Wearing special clothes
medium.explanation: Joshua's complaint means 'what harm have you caused us?' — that is, how have you brought trouble and defilement upon the people.

medium.question: Who was the punishment in these verses directed at?
answers: The whole tribe of Israel
The man who sinned (Achan) alone
Joshua's counselors
medium.explanation: The narrative shows the punishment was carried out on the individual offender, Achan, while the people executed the sentence upon him.

challenge.question: Why might the text record both stoning and burning of the body?
answers: To indicate complete destruction and removal of the defilement from the camp
Because the two events happened many years apart
To show legal equivalence between different groups
challenge.explanation: Combining stoning and burning stresses total destruction and removal of the polluting offense, emphasizing community purification.

challenge.question: What social/cultural purpose did erecting a 'great heap of stones' at that place serve?
answers: A sign of honor and elevated status
A public memorial of the sin and its punishment — a warning to others
A marker of a private property boundary
challenge.explanation: In the biblical context such heaps often served as public memorials; here it memorialized the event and served as a cautionary sign for the future.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'unto this day' at the end of the passage express?
answers: That the event happened briefly and was then forgotten
That the name and memory endured as a lasting reminder up to the time the narrative was written
That the verse is a future prophecy that has not yet occurred
challenge.explanation: 'Unto this day' indicates the name (the Valley of Achor) and the memory of the event continued as a lasting reminder through the generations up to the time of writing.

questions.question: Why might the text record both stoning and burning of the body?
answers: To indicate complete destruction and removal of the defilement from the camp
Because the two events happened many years apart
To show legal equivalence between different groups
questions.explanation: Combining stoning and burning stresses total destruction and removal of the polluting offense, emphasizing community purification.

questions.question: What social/cultural purpose did erecting a 'great heap of stones' at that place serve?
answers: A sign of honor and elevated status
A public memorial of the sin and its punishment — a warning to others
A marker of a private property boundary
questions.explanation: In the biblical context such heaps often served as public memorials; here it memorialized the event and served as a cautionary sign for the future.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'unto this day' at the end of the passage express?
answers: That the event happened briefly and was then forgotten
That the name and memory endured as a lasting reminder up to the time the narrative was written
That the verse is a future prophecy that has not yet occurred
questions.explanation: 'Unto this day' indicates the name (the Valley of Achor) and the memory of the event continued as a lasting reminder through the generations up to the time of writing.
